where: Section 3, last paragraph ("The 8086 SHORT jump is relative; NEAR and FAR jumps are absolute...")
problem: Says 8086 NEAR jumps are absolute. A same-segment NEAR JMP assembles to a 16-bit displacement counted from the address of the next instruction; it is relative, not absolute. Only the FAR JMP carries a full CS:IP absolute address (and indirect near jumps take the target from a register or memory). A student will wrongly think a NEAR jump stores a full offset.
fix: The 8086 SHORT jump stores an 8-bit displacement and the NEAR jump a 16-bit displacement, both counted from the address of the next instruction, so both are relative. A FAR jump carries a full CS:IP address and is absolute. Choose relative for nearby code and absolute for fixed addresses such as interrupt vectors.

problem: JP means "jump if positive (S = 0)" on the 8085 but "jump if parity even (P = 1)" on the 8086. The chapter lists both meanings without warning that the same mnemonic flips meaning, and a student revising quickly can carry the 8085 meaning over to the 8086.
fix: Add one line: on the 8085 JP tests S = 0 (positive) and JPE tests parity; on the 8086 JP/JPE both mean parity even and the sign jumps are JS/JNS. Check the mnemonic against the CPU, not from memory.

problem: "keeps the upper 5 bits of PC" is ambiguous: those 5 bits come from the address of the instruction after the 2-byte AJMP, not from the AJMP's own address. An AJMP placed across a 2 KB boundary will not reach the page a student expects.
fix: AJMP stores 11 address bits (A10-A0) and takes the upper 5 bits from the address of the next instruction, so the target must lie in the same 2 KB page as the instruction after the AJMP.
